why: E-mail is the channel a company owns: no algorithm decides who sees it, and it usually brings the best return for people who already know the brand. CRM and automation tools (HubSpot, Salesforce, Brevo, Mailchimp, Klaviyo) are asked for in most marketing and growth roles.
outcome: build a list legally, set up a domain so e-mails reach the inbox, write and test campaigns, read e-mail metrics honestly, design automated flows, organize contacts in a CRM with lifecycle stages and score leads for sales.

lessons.title: Building a list with consent
text: An e-mail list is built, never bought. Under the GDPR, marketing e-mails to individuals need their consent: a box they tick themselves (not pre-ticked), with a clear purpose, and proof of when and how they agreed. In France, the CNIL allows one exception for existing customers: e-mails about similar products, if they could refuse at the time and can unsubscribe in every message (soft opt-in).

For business contacts (B2B), a professional address may receive offers related to the person’s job, if they were told and can object easily. Every message must say who sends it and offer a simple unsubscribe.
points: Ask for consent where people see value: a guide, a size chart, a newsletter with a clear promise.
Double opt-in (a confirmation e-mail) gives cleaner lists and proof of consent.
Never buy or rent lists: no consent, many traps, and damage to your sender reputation.
Keep consent records: date, source, wording shown.

lessons.title: Deliverability: reaching the inbox
text: Mailbox providers decide whether an e-mail lands in the inbox, the promotions tab or spam, from the sender’s authentication and reputation. Authenticate your domain: SPF lists the servers allowed to send for it, DKIM signs each message, and DMARC tells receivers what to do when checks fail and sends you reports.

Since February 2024, Gmail and Yahoo require bulk senders (more than 5,000 messages a day to Gmail) to have SPF, DKIM and DMARC, a one-click unsubscribe honoured within two days, and a spam complaint rate below 0.3 % (Google advises staying under 0.1 %).
points: Send from your own domain, not a free address.
Remove hard bounces at once and inactive contacts after a re-engagement attempt.
Warm up a new domain or IP slowly: small volumes to the most engaged first.
Watch Google Postmaster Tools for spam rate and domain reputation.

example.code:
; DNS records for stridelab.example (sending through an e-mail platform)
stridelab.example.          TXT  "v=spf1 include:_spf.mailplatform.example ~all"
s1._domainkey.stridelab.example. CNAME s1.dkim.mailplatform.example.
_dmarc.stridelab.example.   TXT  "v=DMARC1; p=none; rua=mailto:dmarc@stridelab.example"
example.note: Start DMARC with p=none to collect reports, then move to quarantine or reject when every sender is authenticated.

lessons.title: Writing e-mails that get read
text: The sender name and the subject line decide the open; the first lines and the call to action decide the click. Write one main message per e-mail, with one primary button, a clear benefit and a reason to act now. The preheader (preview text) completes the subject.

Design for mobile first: one column, a large button, readable text without images (many clients block them), alt text, and a plain-text version. Personalize with what you really know (first purchase, interest chosen), not only the first name.
points: Subject lines: short, specific, honest; avoid all capitals and false urgency.
Test subject lines and calls to action with an A/B test on part of the list.
Send a test to several mail clients and check every link has UTM tags.
A consistent sender and rhythm build trust: tell people how often you write.

example.code:
From: StrideLab <news@stridelab.example>
Subject: Your size guide is ready (and 10 % off this week)
List-Unsubscribe: <https://stridelab.example/unsub?u=8f3a2c>, <mailto:unsub@stridelab.example?subject=u-8f3a2c>
List-Unsubscribe-Post: List-Unsubscribe=One-Click
example.note: List-Unsubscribe with List-Unsubscribe-Post gives the one-click unsubscribe button Gmail and Yahoo require.

lessons.title: E-mail metrics, honestly
text: Read the metrics from the bottom of the funnel up. Delivery rate and bounces show list health; clicks and the click rate show interest; conversions and revenue per e-mail show business value; unsubscribes and spam complaints show fatigue.

Open rates have been unreliable since Apple Mail Privacy Protection (2021) loads images automatically for many users: opens are inflated. Use clicks and conversions to compare campaigns, and opens only as a rough trend.
points: Hard bounce: the address does not exist (remove it). Soft bounce: temporary (full box, server down).
Click-to-open rate compares clicks with opens: careful, it inherits the open problem.
Revenue per recipient compares campaigns of different sizes.
A rising unsubscribe rate after a frequency change is a signal, not a disaster.

example.code:
Campaign: November newsletter, 20,000 sent
Delivered         19,600   (98 %; 400 bounces: 150 hard, 250 soft)
Unique clicks        784   (4.0 % of delivered)
Orders                47   (6.0 % of clickers)
Unsubscribes          59   (0.3 %)
Spam complaints       12   (0.06 %)
example.note: Complaints at 0.06 % are under Google’s 0.1 % advice; the 150 hard bounces must be removed before the next send.

lessons.title: Automation: flows that run on their own
text: Marketing automation sends the right message when a person does something, without anyone pressing send. A flow starts with a trigger (sign-up, cart abandoned, purchase, date, score reached), then waits, checks conditions and sends e-mails or other actions (SMS, task for sales, change of stage).

The flows that earn the most are usually: the welcome series, cart and browse abandonment, the post-purchase series (thank you, how to use, review request, next product), re-engagement of inactive contacts and win-back of lost customers.
points: Every flow needs an exit: a buyer should not receive the 'you forgot your cart' e-mail.
Limit the total number of e-mails a person can receive per week across all flows.
Measure each flow against a control group when possible.
Review flows every quarter: products, prices and links change.

example.code:
Trigger : added to cart, no purchase within 1 hour
  ├─ Wait 1 h  → E-mail 1 "You left something behind" (product, photo, link back to the cart)
  ├─ Wait 24 h → purchased? yes → exit
  │            no  → E-mail 2 reviews of the product + free returns
  └─ Wait 48 h → purchased? yes → exit
               no  → E-mail 3 last reminder (a small offer only if margin allows)
Exit    : purchase, unsubscribe, or 3 e-mails sent
example.note: Three steps, an exit at each step, and a discount only at the end and only if the margin allows.

lessons.title: The CRM and the customer lifecycle
text: A CRM (customer relationship management: HubSpot, Salesforce, Brevo, Zoho, Pipedrive) holds every contact, company and deal, with their history: forms, e-mails, meetings, purchases. Marketing and sales share it, so everyone sees the same customer.

Lifecycle stages describe where a contact is: subscriber, lead, marketing qualified lead (MQL), sales qualified lead (SQL), opportunity, customer, evangelist. Clear definitions agreed with sales (a service level agreement: who follows up what, how fast) avoid the classic quarrel about lead quality.
points: Keep data clean: required fields, no duplicates, consistent values (country lists, job levels).
Segment on behaviour and value, not only demographics (RFM: recency, frequency, monetary value).
Sync the CRM with the e-mail tool and the ad platforms (customer lists, offline conversions).
Only collect the data you use, and say why in the privacy policy.

lessons.title: Lead scoring and nurturing
text: Lead scoring gives points to contacts so sales call the right ones first. Fit points describe who they are (job, company size, country); behaviour points describe what they do (pricing page, demo request, webinar). Negative points remove students, competitors and contacts gone quiet.

Contacts below the threshold receive nurturing: a series of useful content matched to their stage and interest, until they are ready. Check the model with sales every quarter: do high scores really become customers?
points: Start simple: a few rules that sales agree with, then adjust from results.
A demo request goes to sales at once, whatever the score.
Scores should decay with time: interest from six months ago is cold.
Measure MQL → SQL → customer rates to see where leads are lost.

example.code:
Fit (who they are)                      Behaviour (what they do)
Job title is HR manager or director +15  Visited the pricing page        +20
Company of 50-500 people            +10  Requested a demo                +40
Country in the sales area           +5   Opened 3 e-mails in 30 days     +5
Student or competitor e-mail domain -30  No activity for 60 days         -15

Score >= 50  → marketing qualified lead (MQL), sent to sales
example.note: Fit and behaviour scores kept separate show whether a lead is the right person, interested now, or both.

items: The person ticked the box themselves
Confirmed by clicking a link in an e-mail
Existing customers, similar products, easy refusal
In every message, simple, honoured quickly
Servers allowed to send for the domain
Signature that proves the message was not changed
Policy when SPF or DKIM fail, plus reports
Address does not exist: remove it
Inflated by Apple Mail Privacy Protection
The event that starts a flow
Lead approved by marketing / accepted by sales

pitfalls: Buying a list or adding contacts who never agreed.
Judging campaigns on open rates since Apple Mail Privacy Protection.
Automated flows with no exit, which keep chasing people who already bought.
Sending more often without watching unsubscribes and complaints.
A scoring model that sales never agreed with, so MQLs are ignored.

exercises.q: Match each DNS record with what it does.
pairs: Lists the servers allowed to send for the domain
Signs each message so receivers can check it
Says what to do when checks fail and sends reports
exercises.answer: Gmail and Yahoo require all three from bulk senders since February 2024.

exercises.q: Since Apple Mail Privacy Protection, which metric should you use first to compare two newsletters?
options: Number of contacts on the list
Number of images in the e-mail
exercises.answer: Apple Mail loads images (and the tracking pixel) automatically for many users, so opens are inflated. Clicks and conversions are real actions.

exercises.q: Put the CRM lifecycle stages in order.
exercises.answer: Each stage has a definition agreed with sales; the conversion rate between stages shows where leads are lost.

exercises.q: Sort these lead scoring rules into fit and behaviour.
exercises.answer: Fit says whether the contact is the right buyer; behaviour says whether they are interested now. A good lead has both.

exercises.q: A newsletter was delivered to 19,600 people and got 784 unique clicks. What is the click rate in percent?
exercises.answer: 784 / 19,600 = 4 %. Use delivered (not sent) as the base: bounces never had a chance to be clicked.

exercises.q: Your spam complaint rate jumped to 0.4 % after you imported 8,000 contacts from a trade show. What do you do?

choices.label: Stop sending to the imported contacts
choices.feedback: Above 0.3 %, Gmail may send your e-mails to spam for everyone, including your best customers.

choices.label: Send them more e-mails so they get used to the brand
choices.feedback: More unwanted e-mails mean more complaints and a worse reputation.

steps.text: How do you bring them back properly?

choices.label: One permission e-mail asking them to confirm, then keep only those who click
choices.feedback: A re-permission campaign gives consent and keeps the domain reputation safe.

choices.label: Change the sending domain
choices.feedback: Hiding behind a new domain does not fix consent and is seen as spammer behaviour.

exercises.answer: Stop the source of complaints, ask for consent with one clear permission e-mail, keep those who confirm, and watch Google Postmaster Tools until the spam rate is back under 0.1 %.

exercises.q: Design a welcome series for a cosmetics shop newsletter: number of e-mails, timing, and the goal of each one.
exercises.answer: Example, 4 e-mails over 10 days: day 0, welcome and what to expect (frequency, content) with the promised gift or code; day 2, the brand story and best-sellers with reviews; day 5, a quiz or guide to choose products for one’s skin type (and save the answer as a CRM property); day 9, a reminder that the welcome code expires soon. Exit the series as soon as the person buys; measure clicks, first orders and unsubscribes per e-mail.

interview.q: What did Gmail and Yahoo change for senders in 2024?
interview.a: Bulk senders must authenticate with SPF, DKIM and DMARC, offer a one-click unsubscribe honoured within two days, and keep spam complaints below 0.3 %. All senders need at least SPF or DKIM and valid DNS.

interview.q: Can you send marketing e-mails to a list bought from a supplier?
interview.a: No in practice: the people did not consent to us, it breaks the GDPR rules for consumer e-mail, the lists hold spam traps, and the complaints would damage our domain reputation for every other e-mail.

interview.q: Why are open rates no longer a good metric?
interview.a: Since Apple Mail Privacy Protection, images are often loaded automatically, which counts an open even when nobody read the e-mail. I compare clicks, conversions and revenue per recipient instead.

interview.q: What automated flows would you set up first for an online shop?
interview.a: Welcome series, abandoned cart, post-purchase (thank you, tips, review request, cross-sell) and re-engagement of inactive subscribers, each with exit conditions and a weekly sending cap.

interview.q: What is the difference between an MQL and an SQL?
interview.a: An MQL fits the target and showed enough interest for marketing to pass it on; an SQL has been checked by sales, who agree it is a real sales opportunity. The rate from MQL to SQL shows whether scoring works.

interview.q: How would you keep a CRM clean?
interview.a: Required fields and picklists instead of free text, duplicate rules, regular removal of bounces and inactive contacts, one owner for the data model, and only the fields we really use.
